question: A 3-year-old girl with no significant past medical history presents to the clinic with a 4-day history of acute onset cough. Her parents have recently started to introduce several new foods into her diet. Her vital signs are all within normal limits. Physical exam is significant for decreased breath sounds on the right. What is the most appropriate definitive management in this patient?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "3-year-old girl with acute cough" -> "possible foreign body aspiration" -> "decreased breath sounds on the right" -> "need to visualize airway" -> "flexible bronchoscopy is appropriate" -> 85%

CHAIN: "3-year-old girl with acute cough" -> "recent introduction of new foods" -> "possible allergic reaction or aspiration" -> "decreased breath sounds on the right" -> "need to assess for obstruction" -> "rigid bronchoscopy may be needed" -> 80%

CHAIN: "3-year-old girl with acute cough" -> "decreased breath sounds on the right" -> "possible pneumonia or foreign body" -> "chest x-ray can help differentiate" -> "CXR may not be definitive" -> "flexible bronchoscopy is more definitive" -> 75%
CHAIN: "3-year-old girl with acute cough" -> "decreased breath sounds on the right" -> "possible aspiration" -> "need for airway intervention" -> "flexible bronchoscopy is the best option" -> 90%
analysis: The acute onset cough and decreased breath sounds on the right in a 3-year-old girl suggest the possibility of a foreign body aspiration, especially given the recent introduction of new foods. Rigid bronchoscopy is the definitive management for foreign body removal in children, as it allows for direct visualization and retrieval of the object. Other options like CXR or bronchodilators may be useful for diagnosis or symptomatic relief but do not provide definitive management.
